2 Introduction

This vignette demonstrates the ForestSearch methodology for exploratory subgroup identification with a binary outcome on the odds-ratio (OR) scale, applied to the ACTG175 trial. It uses the GLM extension of ForestSearch (León et al. 2024 Statistics in Medicine) and is the binary-outcome counterpart to the continuous-outcome vignette.

2.1 Motivation

Many randomized trials have binary endpoints (response, improvement, event-by-time-point indicators) where the natural treatment-effect contrast is the odds ratio between arms. ForestSearch identifies subgroups where the treatment effect deviates meaningfully from a prespecified threshold, with proper accounting for the optimism inherent in data-driven subgroup discovery.

2.2 Methodology Overview — Dual-Scale Framing

Note

ForestSearch vs GRF: The forestsearch methodology was developed for survival data where the outcome is generally the timing to an adverse outcome and thresholds (e.g., indicative of harm) were defined accordingly. In contrast, GRF evaluates data in terms of benefit where thresholds are defined as benefit in favor of control. The dual-scale framing is simply a matter of aligning the threshold directions (for harm) to the forestsearch and GRF interpretations.

This analysis applies two different methods on two different scales of the same binary outcome:

  • Part I — ForestSearch on the adverse scale (y_binary_neg = 1 - y_binary_pos, indicator of NO CD4 improvement; 1 = worse). With adverse_outcome = TRUE, an OR above the screening threshold indicates harm (the treatment increases the odds of no improvement).
  • Part II — GRF standalone on the beneficial scale (y_binary_pos = I(cd420 > cd40), indicator of CD4 improvement; 1 = better). With the default adverse_outcome = FALSE, a CATE below the threshold indicates harm (insufficient improvement).
  • Part III — Cross-method comparison: per-subject H/Hc agreement between the two analyses, with Cohen’s κ.

The two scales are sign-flipped versions of the same binary outcome (y_binary_neg = 1 - y_binary_pos), so the ITT log-odds-ratios are equal in magnitude with opposite signs. Differences in identified subgroups reflect the methods (FS exhaustive search vs GRF policy tree) and the model class, not the data.

2.3 Trial Background

ACTG175 (Hammer et al. 1996) randomized HIV-positive patients with CD4 counts of 200–500 per mm³ to four treatment arms. This analysis uses the two pure-monotherapy arms:

  • Arm 1: ZDV + ddI combination therapy (treatment, T = 1)
  • Arm 3: ddI monotherapy (control, T = 0)

The outcome is the change in CD4 count from baseline to week 20 (cd40 → cd420).

# Set ggplot theme
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

3.2 Analysis Parameters

# ─── Parallel processing ────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_cores <- max(1L, floor(0.95 * parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)))

# ─── Reproducibility ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
analysis_seed <- 8316951L
set.seed(analysis_seed)

# ─── Confounders ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cont_vars <- c("age", "preanti", "wtkg", "karnof", "cd40", "cd80")
bin_vars  <- c("hemo", "homo", "drugs", "race", "gender", "symptom")
confounders.name <- c(cont_vars, bin_vars)
id.name <- "id"

# ─── Variables (dual-scale framing) ────────────────────────────────────
treat.name         <- "treat"
adverse_outcome    <- "y_binary_neg"   # FS adverse-scale outcome
beneficial_outcome <- "y_binary_pos"   # GRF beneficial-scale outcome

# ─── ForestSearch parameters (binary, OR scale) ────────────────────────
fs_outcome_type    <- "binary"
fs_effect_measure  <- "OR"

fs_sg_focus        <- "effMaxSG"   # GLM-natural alias for "hrMaxSG" (see
                                   # NEWS for the effect-vocabulary aliases)
fs_selection_rule  <- "both"   # candidate inclusion: neighborhood ∩ Pareto
                               # (only used by effMaxSG / effMinSG focus)

# Thresholds on the OR scale (adverse scale: OR > c1 = harm)
fs_or_threshold    <- 1.25  # screening: OR >= 1.25 indicates harm
fs_or_consistency  <- 1.0   # consistency: OR >= 1.0 (nominal harm)

fs_pconsistency    <- 0.80
fs_n_min           <- 60L
fs_d0_min          <- 10L
fs_d1_min          <- 10L
fs_splits          <- 500L
fs_max_subgroups   <- 20
fs_maxk            <- 2L
fs_use_lasso       <- TRUE
fs_use_grf         <- TRUE
fs_is_RCT          <- TRUE
fs_vi_grf_min      <- -0.2
fs_dmin_grf        <- 0
fs_cont_cutoff     <- 4L

# ─── Pareto-frontier diagnostic parameters ──────────────────────────────
# Drives compute_frontier_cis(), plot_pareto_frontier(),
# pareto_frontier_table(), and explain_pareto_selection() in the
# post-hoc selection diagnostic section.
# NB: with sg_focus = "effMaxSG" and selection_rule = "both", the rule
# selects from the intersection of the effect-size neighborhood (within
# `effect_neighborhood` of the maximum) and the Pareto-non-dominated set
# on (effect, N).  The selected subgroup is typically a frontier member.
# The frontier is shown here both as the selection criterion AND as a
# diagnostic of the candidate trade-off space.
# For OR (ratio-scale), the effect axis is auto-rendered on log scale
# by plot_pareto_frontier(); leave xlim = NULL for auto bounds.
frontier_params <- list(
  n_splits      = 1000L,
  seed          = 1L,
  xlim          = c(0.35,10),       # auto (OR auto-detected as ratio scale)
  digits        = 2L
)

# ─── GRF standalone parameters (beneficial scale) ──────────────────────
grf_outcome_type   <- "binary"
grf_effect_measure <- "OR"
grf_dmin_grf       <- 0.1    # on the RD scale for binary outcomes
                             # (e.g., 0.10 = 10 percentage-point absolute
                             # difference in event rates)
grf_maxdepth       <- 2L
grf_RCT            <- TRUE
grf_sg_criterion   <- "mDiff"
grf_tune           <- FALSE

# ─── Bootstrap (gated; demo by default) ────────────────────────────────
run_bootstrap <- TRUE
NB <- 20L     # PRESSURE-TEST DEMO. Set to 500-2000 for production.

# ─── Cross-Validation (gated; demo by default) ─────────────────────────
run_cv <- TRUE
Kfolds_cv <- 10L  # PRESSURE-TEST DEMO. 10-fold CV. For LOO, set to nrow(fs_result$df.est).
                  # Production: 10-fold is standard; consider forestsearch_tenfold()
                  # with sims = 50-100 for repeated K-fold stability assessment.

# ─── Leave-One-Out CV (gated; demo by default) ─────────────────────────
# LOO runs forestsearch() once per observation (N folds).  Comparable in
# cost to K-fold * N/K, but well-tolerated on samples up to ~1000.
# Set FALSE to skip; toggles independently of run_cv.
run_loo <- FALSE

# ─── Numeric Precision ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Two-stage precision control (Reading-C design):
# - construction_digits: upstream sprintf precision in the bootstrap and
#   CV table builders. Acts as a CEILING for downstream display: values
#   rounded here cannot be recovered later. Default 4 provides headroom.
# - display_digits: precision rendered in user-facing tables.
#   summarize_bootstrap_results() parses construction-time strings and
#   reformats at this precision, which must be <= construction_digits.
#   sg_tables() applies it via ndecimals; cv_summary_tables() applies
#   it via digits.
construction_digits <- 2L
display_digits      <- 2L

# ─── Combined Forest Plot ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Capstone visualization that integrates fs_result, fs_bc (if bootstrap),
# and fs_kfold_result (if CV).  Always rendered; CV/bootstrap annotations
# appear conditionally on the run_* flags.
run_forestplot <- TRUE

4 Data Preparation

4.1 Treatment Assignment

Show code 
# ACTG175: arm 1 = ZDV+ddI (experimental), arm 3 = ddI (control)
actg_df <- subset(speff2trial::ACTG175, arms %in% c(1L, 3L))
actg_df$id <- seq_len(nrow(actg_df))

# Treatment: ZDV+ddI = 1, ddI = 0 (NO switching)
actg_df$treat <- ifelse(actg_df$arms == 1L, 1L, 0L)

4.2 Outcome Construction

Show code 
# Drop subjects missing the week-20 CD4 measurement
actg_df <- actg_df[!is.na(actg_df$cd420), ]

# Beneficial scale: CD4 improvement indicator (1 = improved, higher = better)
actg_df$y_binary_pos <- as.integer(actg_df$cd420 > actg_df$cd40)

# Adverse scale: NO improvement indicator (1 = did not improve, higher = worse)
actg_df$y_binary_neg <- 1L - actg_df$y_binary_pos

outcome_vars <- c("y_binary_neg", "y_binary_pos")

4.3 Covariates

Show code 
# Coerce binary indicators to factors (analyst does not know true cuts
# for continuous covariates; ForestSearch handles those internally)
for (v in bin_vars) actg_df[[v]] <- as.factor(actg_df[[v]])

cat("Continuous candidates:", paste(cont_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
#> Continuous candidates: age, preanti, wtkg, karnof, cd40, cd80
Show code 
cat("Binary candidates:    ", paste(bin_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
#> Binary candidates:     hemo, homo, drugs, race, gender, symptom

4.5 ITT Analysis

Show code 
# Adverse-scale ITT OR (y_binary_neg = no improvement; OR > 1 = treatment
# increases the odds of no improvement = harm)
itt_neg <- glm(y_binary_neg ~ treat, data = actg_df, family = binomial)

# Beneficial-scale ITT OR (y_binary_pos = improvement; OR > 1 = treatment
# increases the odds of improvement = benefit)
itt_pos <- glm(y_binary_pos ~ treat, data = actg_df, family = binomial)

# Helper to print OR / log-OR / 95% CI / p-value
print_or <- function(fit, label) {
  beta  <- coef(fit)["treat"]
  se    <- summary(fit)$coefficients["treat", "Std. Error"]
  z     <- beta / se
  p     <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
  or    <- exp(beta)
  ci_lo <- exp(beta - qnorm(0.975) * se)
  ci_hi <- exp(beta + qnorm(0.975) * se)
  cat(sprintf("=== ITT Odds Ratio, %s ===\n", label))
  cat(sprintf("  log-OR (treat): %7.4f  (SE %.4f)\n", beta, se))
  cat(sprintf("  OR:             %6.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
              or, ci_lo, ci_hi))
  cat(sprintf("  p-value:        %.4f\n", p))
}

print_or(itt_neg, "adverse scale (y_binary_neg)")
#> === ITT Odds Ratio, adverse scale (y_binary_neg) ===
#>   log-OR (treat): -0.4078  (SE 0.1252)
#>   OR:              0.665  (95% CI: 0.520, 0.850)
#>   p-value:        0.0011
Show code 
cat("\n")
Show code 
print_or(itt_pos, "beneficial scale (y_binary_pos)")
#> === ITT Odds Ratio, beneficial scale (y_binary_pos) ===
#>   log-OR (treat):  0.4078  (SE 0.1252)
#>   OR:              1.504  (95% CI: 1.176, 1.922)
#>   p-value:        0.0011
Show code 
cat("\nNote: y_binary_neg = 1 - y_binary_pos, so the two log-ORs are\n")
#> 
#> Note: y_binary_neg = 1 - y_binary_pos, so the two log-ORs are
Show code

5 Part I: ForestSearch (Adverse Scale)

5.1 Rationale

ForestSearch operates on the adverse scale (y_binary_neg, indicator of NO improvement) with adverse_outcome = TRUE. An OR above fs_or_threshold indicates the treatment increases the odds of no improvement in that subgroup (harm). No outcome flip is applied; the screening threshold is on the OR scale directly.

5.2 ForestSearch Parameters

Note

API note: GLM-natural vocabulary. This template uses the GLM-natural parameter names introduced in forestsearch 0.2.0:

  • sg_focus = "effMaxSG" (alias for the legacy "hrMaxSG")
  • effect.threshold (alias for hr.threshold)
  • consistency.threshold (alias for hr.consistency)

The "eff*" and effect.* forms read more naturally for GLM outcomes (continuous MD, binary OR/RR/RD, count IRR) where there is no hazard ratio. The legacy "hr*" and hr.* forms continue to work and produce identical results. See NEWS.md for the full list of aliases.

Parameter Value Description
effect_measure OR Odds ratio (binary)
effect.threshold 1.25 Screening OR threshold (adverse scale)
consistency.threshold 1.0 Per-split consistency OR threshold
pconsistency.threshold 0.80 Required consistency rate across splits
maxk 2 Maximum factors per subgroup
n.min 60 Minimum subgroup size
d0.min, d1.min 10 Minimum sample size per arm
fs.splits 500 Random 50/50 splits for consistency
sg_focus effMaxSG Effect-neighborhood focus (max-N tiebreaker)
selection_rule both Intersection of neighborhood and Pareto sets

5.3 Running ForestSearch

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()

fs_result <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis      = actg_df,
  confounders.name = confounders.name,
  outcome.name     = adverse_outcome,
  event.name       = adverse_outcome,    # binary: outcome IS the event
  treat.name       = treat.name,
  id.name          = id.name,
  # GLM parameters
  outcome_type     = fs_outcome_type,
  effect_measure   = fs_effect_measure,
  adverse_outcome  = TRUE,
  seedit           = analysis_seed,
  # Threshold parameters (OR scale)
  effect.threshold       = fs_or_threshold,
  consistency.threshold  = fs_or_consistency,
  pconsistency.threshold = fs_pconsistency,
  # Search configuration
  sg_focus         = fs_sg_focus,
  selection_rule   = fs_selection_rule,
  max_subgroups_search = fs_max_subgroups,
  use_twostage     = TRUE,    
  conf.cont_jcuts           = list(cd40 = 10, wtkg = 10),
  # Factor selection
  use_grf          = fs_use_grf,
  return_selected_cuts_only = TRUE,
  use_lasso        = fs_use_lasso,
  cut_type         = "default",
  # Subgroup constraints
  maxk             = fs_maxk,
  n.min            = fs_n_min,
  d0.min           = fs_d0_min,
  d1.min           = fs_d1_min,
  # Consistency evaluation
  fs.splits        = fs_splits,
  # Parallel processing
  parallel_args    = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  ),
  # Output options
  show_candidate_summary = TRUE,
  details          = TRUE,
  plot.sg          = FALSE,    # KM not applicable; use plot_sg_glm_outcomes()
  is.RCT           = fs_is_RCT,
  vi.grf.min       = fs_vi_grf_min,
  dmin.grf         = fs_dmin_grf,
  cont.cutoff      = fs_cont_cutoff,
  tune_grf         = grf_tune,
  quiet            = FALSE
)

5.8 Selection Diagnostic: Pareto Frontier

Post-hoc diagnostic showing all passing candidates on the (OR, N) plane.

Note

Context for sg_focus = "effMaxSG" with selection_rule = "both". The rule selects from the intersection of two sets: candidates within effect_neighborhood of the maximum effect (the “in-band” set), AND candidates on the Pareto frontier in (effect, N). Among that intersection, the rule picks the largest-N candidate.

The selected subgroup is therefore typically a frontier member, and the frontier plot serves both as the selection geometry AND as a diagnostic showing the alternatives the rule considered (and ruled out). Compare this to the comparison vignette, which shows what happens when selection_rule is varied with all else fixed.

For OR outcomes the effect axis is auto-rendered on log scale by plot_pareto_frontier() and pareto_frontier_table() (auto-detected from fs_result$effect_measure); the rendered values are on the natural OR scale.

Show code 
# Formatted gt table; selected subgroup is highlighted and marked with ★.
# Works uniformly for survival (HR) and GLM (OR, RR, IRR, RD, IRD, MD)
# outcomes — effect-column label and scale derived from
# fs_result$effect_measure.  For OR, the effect column is exponentiated
# for display and the band test is on the natural OR scale.

# 1. Compute the CIs once (this is the expensive step, ~1-3 min).
#    Parameters come from frontier_params in the Analysis Configuration.
ci_tab <- compute_frontier_cis(
  fs_result,
  n_splits = frontier_params$n_splits,
  seed     = frontier_params$seed
)

# 2. Plot, with split-derived CI bars overlaid; same intervals as the table.
p_pareto <- plot_pareto_frontier(
  fs_result,
  ci_table  = ci_tab,
  show_band = TRUE,
  xlim      = frontier_params$xlim
)
print(p_pareto)
Show code 
# 3. Render the table. Pass the same ci_tab so the table and plot show
#    identical intervals.
pareto_frontier_table(
  fs_result,
  ci_table = ci_tab,
  digits   = frontier_params$digits
)

5.8.1 Selection Narrative

explain_pareto_selection() describes the chosen subgroup relative to the non-dominated alternatives on the frontier. Under effMaxSG with selection_rule = "both", the winner is a frontier member that also sits in the effect-size band; the “losers” are frontier candidates that fall outside the band (high-N candidates with weaker effect). The narrative names both the criterion and the runner-up.

Show code 
cat(explain_pareto_selection(fs_result, ci_table = ci_tab))

Selection criterion. The configured criterion is largest-N within the effect-size band (sg_focus = “hrMaxSG”) under the intersection of effect-band and Pareto-non-dominance rules. The effect-size band requires odds ratio within 10% of the maximum on the frontier (i.e., odds ratio >= 5.703). Within the eligible set, ties on N are broken by Pcons, then by effect strength, then by parsimony (smaller K).

Selected subgroup. !{wtkg <= 83.4624} AND !{cd40 <= 413} (odds ratio = 6.337, N = 71, Pcons = 1.000, K = 2). This is the largest-N candidate in the eligible set among non-dominated frontier candidates. The Naive 95% CI for the odds ratio on this subgroup is (2.186, 18.367).

Non-selected frontier candidates (ordered by closeness to winning):

  • !{wtkg <= 83.4624} AND !{cd40 <= 390} (odds ratio = 4.921, N = 83, Pcons = 1.000, K = 2). fell outside the effect-size band (odds ratio = 4.921 below the floor); excluded before the N tiebreaker even applies.

  • !{wtkg <= 83.4624} AND !{cd40 <= 379.5} (odds ratio = 2.879, N = 97, Pcons = 0.940, K = 2). fell outside the effect-size band (odds ratio = 2.879 below the floor); excluded before the N tiebreaker even applies.

  • !{cd40 <= 390} AND !{wtkg <= 81.2} (odds ratio = 2.564, N = 104, Pcons = 1.000, K = 2). fell outside the effect-size band (odds ratio = 2.564 below the floor); excluded before the N tiebreaker even applies.

  • !{cd40 <= 320.8} AND !{wtkg <= 85.5} (odds ratio = 1.913, N = 112, Pcons = 0.940, K = 2). fell outside the effect-size band (odds ratio = 1.913 below the floor); excluded before the N tiebreaker even applies.

  • !{wtkg <= 81.2} AND !{cd40 <= 379.5} (odds ratio = 1.813, N = 122, Pcons = 0.890, K = 2). fell outside the effect-size band (odds ratio = 1.813 below the floor); excluded before the N tiebreaker even applies.

  • !{wtkg <= 83.4624} AND !{cd40 <= 320.8} (odds ratio = 1.748, N = 137, Pcons = 0.970, K = 2). fell outside the effect-size band (odds ratio = 1.748 below the floor); excluded before the N tiebreaker even applies.

Show code 
# Programmatic access — two paths.

# (a) Frontier table with pre-formatted CI strings, one row per frontier
#     member.  CI columns ("Naive 95% CI", "Split ~ 95% CI",
#     "FSBC ~ 95% CI") are character strings like "(1.45, 2.87)".
pareto_frontier_table(
  fs_result,
  ci_table = ci_tab,
  format   = "data.table",
  digits   = frontier_params$digits
)

# (b) Rich post-consistency view: ALL passing candidates (not just the
#     frontier), with on_frontier and (where applicable) in_band flag
#     columns added.  Provides programmatic access to the same content
#     as the in-flight summary printed by forestsearch().
pareto_frontier_table(
  fs_result,
  ci_table          = ci_tab,
  include_dominated = TRUE,
  format            = "data.table",
  digits            = frontier_params$digits
)

# (c) Raw numeric CIs: keyed data.table with one row per frontier
#     member.  Same content as (a) but each bound is a numeric column
#     (naive_lcl, naive_ucl, split_lcl, split_ucl, fsbc_estimate,
#     fsbc_lcl, fsbc_ucl, plus split_sd and n_valid_splits).  This is
#     what step 1 of fs-pareto produced.
ci_tab

5.9 Bootstrap Bias Correction

Bootstrap bias correction adjusts the FS point estimate for the optimism inherent in data-driven subgroup identification. The bootstrap pipeline auto-detects the OR effect column from fs_result and produces bias-corrected OR estimates with bootstrap distributions and diagnostics.

Note

Demo mode: NB = 20 for pressure-testing the pipeline end-to-end. Production runs should use NB = 500–2000. Set run_bootstrap = FALSE in the parameters chunk to skip this section entirely.

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()

fs_bc <- forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture(
  fs.est = fs_result,
  nb_boots = NB,
  show_three = FALSE,
  details = FALSE,
  digits = construction_digits,
  parallel_args = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  )
)
#> Warning in forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture(fs.est = fs_result, nb_boots = NB, :
#> nb_boots < 100 may produce unreliable confidence intervals. Recommend at least

5.10 Cross-Validation

K-fold cross-validation assesses the stability of the FS pipeline by re-running ForestSearch on each leave-out fold and comparing the identified subgroup to the full-data analysis. Per-fold results are aggregated into agreement metrics (sensitivity for H and Hc) and finding rates.

Note

Demo mode: Kfolds_cv = 10 for pressure-testing the CV pipeline end-to-end. Production runs typically use 10-fold CV; for repeated K-fold stability assessment, see forestsearch_tenfold(sims = 50, Kfolds = 10). Set run_cv = FALSE in the parameters chunk to skip this section.

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()

fs_kfold_result <- forestsearch_Kfold(
  fs.est        = fs_result,
  Kfolds        = Kfolds_cv,
  seedit        = analysis_seed,
  parallel_args = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  ),
  details       = FALSE
)
#> Parallel plan: multisession with 13 workers.
Show code 
plan("sequential"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
#>           used  (Mb) gc trigger  (Mb) limit (Mb) max used  (Mb)
#> Ncells 3364706 179.7    6024688 321.8         NA  6024688 321.8
#> Vcells 8563555  65.4   19836299 151.4      36864 16463582 125.7
Show code 
timings$cv <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]

cat("\nCross-validation completed in", round(timings$cv / 60, 2), "minutes",
    sprintf("(Kfolds = %d, n_cores = %d)\n", Kfolds_cv, n_cores))
#> 
#> Cross-validation completed in 0.27 minutes (Kfolds = 10, n_cores = 13)

5.11 Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation

Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation is the limiting case of K-fold CV where each observation is held out once. It is the most thorough form of CV, eliminating fold-assignment randomness, and is the appropriate benchmark when sample size is small enough to make N re-fits tractable.

Note

Cost: LOO runs forestsearch() once per observation. Toggleable independently from K-fold via run_loo in the parameters chunk. On samples up to roughly 1000 the cost is well-tolerated with parallel workers; beyond that, K-fold is preferred.

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()

# LOO is triggered by Kfolds = N (the function default behavior at
# forestsearch_cross_validation.R:109).  We pass it explicitly here for
# clarity.
N_loo <- nrow(fs_result$df.est)

fs_loo_result <- forestsearch_Kfold(
  fs.est        = fs_result,
  Kfolds        = N_loo,
  seedit        = analysis_seed,
  parallel_args = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  ),
  details       = FALSE
)

plan("sequential"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
timings$loo <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]

cat("\nLOO completed in", round(timings$loo / 60, 2), "minutes",
    sprintf("(N folds = %d, n_cores = %d)\n", N_loo, n_cores))

5.11.1 LOO Summary

Show code 
cat(cv_summary_text(fs_loo_result, est.scale = "hr"), "\n")
cat(sprintf("Subgroup found in %.0f%% of %d folds.\n",
            100 * fs_loo_result$prop_SG_found, N_loo))

5.11.2 LOO Tables

The cv_summary_tables() helper returns five publication-ready gt tables. The first is the combined ITT + subgroup view; the next three are component estimation tables (ITT, full-analysis subgroup, LOO subgroup) that show the underlying treatment-effect estimates with confidence intervals.

Show code 
loo_out  <- forestsearch_KfoldOut(fs_loo_result, outall = TRUE,
                                  digits = construction_digits)
loo_tabs <- cv_summary_tables(
  loo_out,
  title    = "ACTG175 Leave-One-Out CV Summary (Binary, OR)",
  subtitle = sprintf("ITT and Subgroup Estimates: Full Analysis (FA) vs LOO (N=%d)",
                     N_loo),
  digits   = display_digits,
  use_gt   = TRUE
)

6 Part II: GRF Standalone (Beneficial Scale)

6.1 Rationale

GRF operates on the beneficial scale (y_binary_pos, indicator of CD4 improvement) with adverse_outcome = FALSE (the default). A negative CATE means the treatment decreases the probability of improvement in that subgroup — harm via insufficient benefit. This is the natural complement to the FS analysis on the adverse scale: same outcome data, opposite encoding, and a different model class (causal forest with policy-tree subgroup extraction).

For binary outcomes the per-subject CATE from grf::causal_forest() is on the risk-difference (RD) scale: \(\widehat{\tau}_i = \hat{P}(Y_i=1 \mid T=1, X_i) - \hat{P}(Y_i=1 \mid T=0, X_i)\), bounded in \([-1, 1]\). The dmin.grf threshold is interpreted on this same RD scale (e.g., dmin.grf = 0.10 requires at least a 10 percentage-point absolute difference in event rates). The effect-measure label "OR" controls how the FS-side estimation and reporting step renders the subgroup contrast; the GRF CATE itself remains on the RD scale internally.

6.2 Running GRF

Show code 
t0 <- proc.time()

grf_result <- grf.subg.harm.glm(
  data             = actg_df,
  confounders.name = confounders.name,
  outcome.name     = beneficial_outcome,
  treat.name       = treat.name,
  id.name          = id.name,
  outcome_type     = grf_outcome_type,
  effect_measure   = grf_effect_measure,
  dmin.grf         = grf_dmin_grf,
  maxdepth         = grf_maxdepth,
  RCT              = grf_RCT,
  sg.criterion     = grf_sg_criterion,
  details          = TRUE
)

timings$grf <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]
cat("\nGRF (beneficial scale) completed in",
    round(timings$grf, 1), "seconds\n")
#> 
#> GRF (beneficial scale) completed in 0.3 seconds

6.4 Identified Subgroup Definition

Show code 
if (!is.null(grf_result$sg.harm.id) && length(grf_result$sg.harm.id) > 0) {
  grf_H <- grf_result$data$treat.recommend == 0
  cat("Identified subgroup (H, GRF beneficial):",
      paste(grf_result$sg.harm.id, collapse = " & "), "\n")
  cat(sprintf("Subgroup size: %d (%.1f%% of ITT)\n",
              sum(grf_H), 100 * mean(grf_H)))
  cat(sprintf("CATE(H):  %+6.3f  (RD: P(improve|T=1) - P(improve|T=0) in H)\n",
              grf_result$cate_sg))
  cat(sprintf("CATE(Hc): %+6.3f\n", grf_result$cate_sgc))
} else {
  cat("GRF: no subgroup identified.\n")
}

#> Subgroup size: 130 (12.0% of ITT)

#> CATE(Hc): +0.165

6.5 GRF Variable Importance

GRF reports per-covariate variable importance from the causal forest, quantifying each covariate’s contribution to splitting decisions in the treatment-effect estimation. Higher values indicate stronger influence on detected heterogeneity. Note this differs from prediction-importance in standard random forests; here it reflects relevance to CATE estimation, not to the marginal outcome.

Show code 
if (!is.null(grf_result$grf_varimp) && length(grf_result$grf_varimp) > 0) {
  vi <- grf_result$grf_varimp
  vi_df <- data.frame(
    variable   = names(vi),
    importance = unname(vi)
  )
  # Order ascending so largest appears at top after coord_flip()
  vi_df <- vi_df[order(vi_df$importance), ]
  vi_df$variable <- factor(vi_df$variable, levels = vi_df$variable)

  ggplot(vi_df, aes(x = variable, y = importance)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      x        = NULL,
      y        = "GRF variable importance",
      title    = "GRF Variable Importance",
      subtitle = "Higher = more influence on treatment-effect heterogeneity"
    )
} else {
  cat("GRF variable importance not available.\n")
}

6.6 CATE Distribution

Per-subject conditional average treatment effects (CATE) are estimated from GRF’s double-robust scores: \( \widehat{\tau}i = \Gamma{1,i} - \Gamma_{0,i} \), where \( \Gamma_0 \) and \( \Gamma_1 \) are the doubly robust outcome predictions under control and treatment. For binary outcomes the CATE is on the risk-difference (RD) scale: positive CATE means the treatment increases the probability of improvement (benefit); negative CATE means it decreases the probability (harm via insufficient improvement). The histogram below shows the empirical CATE distribution across subjects, colored by GRF-assigned subgroup membership. Bounded in \([-1, 1]\) in principle, though typical CATE magnitudes are smaller (±0.1 to ±0.3 absolute probability difference).

Show code 
if (!is.null(grf_result$dr_scores) &&
    !is.null(grf_result$data$treat.recommend)) {

  cate_per_subject <- grf_result$dr_scores[, 2L] -
                      grf_result$dr_scores[, 1L]
  group_label <- ifelse(grf_result$data$treat.recommend == 0,
                        "H (questionable)",
                        "H\u1d9c (recommend)")
  cate_df <- data.frame(
    cate  = cate_per_subject,
    group = factor(group_label,
                   levels = c("H (questionable)", "H\u1d9c (recommend)"))
  )

  ggplot(cate_df, aes(x = cate, fill = group)) +
    geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", bins = 30,
                   color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = grf_result$cate_sg,
               linetype = "dotted", color = "coral", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = grf_result$cate_sgc,
               linetype = "dotted", color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(
      "H (questionable)"     = "coral",
      "H\u1d9c (recommend)"  = "steelblue"
    )) +
    labs(
      x        = "Per-subject CATE: P(Y=1|T=1) - P(Y=1|T=0)  (RD scale)",
      y        = "Count",
      title    = "GRF CATE Distribution",
      subtitle = paste0("Dotted lines: subgroup-mean CATE(H) = ",
                        sprintf("%+.3f", grf_result$cate_sg),
                        ", CATE(H\u1d9c) = ",
                        sprintf("%+.3f", grf_result$cate_sgc),
                        ".  Negative CATE = harm via insufficient improvement."),
      fill     = "Subgroup"
    )
} else {
  cat("GRF DR-scores or treat.recommend not available.\n")
}

7 Part III: Cross-Method Comparison

The two analyses define H differently:

  • FS uses the adverse scale (y_binary_neg, OR > c1 = harm).
  • GRF uses the beneficial scale (y_binary_pos, CATE below 0 = harm).

Both classify subjects as H (treat.recommend == 0) when they meet their respective harm criterion, so per-subject membership is directly comparable. The cross-tabulation below reports raw agreement and Cohen’s κ.

Show code 
sg_comparison <- compare_fs_subgroups(
  fs1     = fs_result,
  fs2     = grf_result,
  label1  = "FS (adverse)",
  label2  = "GRF (beneficial)",
  id.name = id.name,
  subgroup_notation = "harm",
  title   = "FS-Adverse vs GRF-Beneficial: Subgroup Membership"
)

# Introduction

This vignette demonstrates the **ForestSearch** methodology for exploratory
subgroup identification with a **binary outcome on the odds-ratio
(OR) scale**, applied to the ACTG175 trial. It uses the GLM extension of
ForestSearch (León et al. 2024 *Statistics in Medicine*) and is the
binary-outcome counterpart to the continuous-outcome vignette.

## Motivation

Many randomized trials have binary endpoints (response, improvement,
event-by-time-point indicators) where the natural treatment-effect contrast
is the odds ratio between arms. ForestSearch identifies subgroups where
the treatment effect deviates meaningfully from a prespecified threshold,
with proper accounting for the optimism inherent in data-driven subgroup
discovery.

## Methodology Overview — Dual-Scale Framing

::: {.callout-note}
**ForestSearch vs GRF**: The forestsearch methodology was developed for 
survival data where the outcome is generally the timing to an adverse outcome 
and thresholds (e.g., indicative of harm) were defined accordingly.  In contrast, 
GRF evaluates data in terms of benefit where thresholds are defined 
as ``benefit in favor of control``.  The dual-scale framing is simply a matter of
aligning the threshold directions (for harm) to the forestsearch and GRF 
interpretations.
:::



This analysis applies **two different methods** on **two different scales
of the same binary outcome**:

- **Part I — ForestSearch on the adverse scale** (`y_binary_neg = 1 - y_binary_pos`,
  indicator of NO CD4 improvement; 1 = worse). With
  `adverse_outcome = TRUE`, an OR above the screening threshold indicates
  harm (the treatment increases the odds of no improvement).
- **Part II — GRF standalone on the beneficial scale**
  (`y_binary_pos = I(cd420 > cd40)`, indicator of CD4 improvement;
  1 = better). With the default `adverse_outcome = FALSE`, a CATE below
  the threshold indicates harm (insufficient improvement).
- **Part III — Cross-method comparison**: per-subject H/Hc agreement
  between the two analyses, with Cohen's κ.

The two scales are sign-flipped versions of the same binary outcome
(`y_binary_neg = 1 - y_binary_pos`), so the ITT log-odds-ratios are
equal in magnitude with opposite signs. Differences in identified
subgroups reflect the methods (FS exhaustive search vs GRF policy tree)
and the model class, not the data.

## Trial Background

ACTG175 (Hammer et al. 1996) randomized HIV-positive patients with CD4
counts of 200–500 per mm³ to four treatment arms. This analysis uses the
two pure-monotherapy arms:

- **Arm 1**: ZDV + ddI combination therapy (treatment, T = 1)
- **Arm 3**: ddI monotherapy (control, T = 0)

The outcome is the change in CD4 count from baseline to week 20 (`cd40` →
`cd420`).

```{r load-packages}
library(forestsearch)
```

## Analysis Parameters

```{r analysis-params}
#| code-fold: false

# ─── Parallel processing ────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_cores <- max(1L, floor(0.95 * parallel::detectCores(logical = FALSE)))

# ─── Reproducibility ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
analysis_seed <- 8316951L
set.seed(analysis_seed)

# ─── Confounders ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
cont_vars <- c("age", "preanti", "wtkg", "karnof", "cd40", "cd80")
bin_vars  <- c("hemo", "homo", "drugs", "race", "gender", "symptom")
confounders.name <- c(cont_vars, bin_vars)
id.name <- "id"

# ─── Variables (dual-scale framing) ────────────────────────────────────
treat.name         <- "treat"
adverse_outcome    <- "y_binary_neg"   # FS adverse-scale outcome
beneficial_outcome <- "y_binary_pos"   # GRF beneficial-scale outcome

# ─── ForestSearch parameters (binary, OR scale) ────────────────────────
fs_outcome_type    <- "binary"
fs_effect_measure  <- "OR"

fs_sg_focus        <- "effMaxSG"   # GLM-natural alias for "hrMaxSG" (see
                                   # NEWS for the effect-vocabulary aliases)
fs_selection_rule  <- "both"   # candidate inclusion: neighborhood ∩ Pareto
                               # (only used by effMaxSG / effMinSG focus)

# Thresholds on the OR scale (adverse scale: OR > c1 = harm)
fs_or_threshold    <- 1.25  # screening: OR >= 1.25 indicates harm
fs_or_consistency  <- 1.0   # consistency: OR >= 1.0 (nominal harm)

fs_pconsistency    <- 0.80
fs_n_min           <- 60L
fs_d0_min          <- 10L
fs_d1_min          <- 10L
fs_splits          <- 500L
fs_max_subgroups   <- 20
fs_maxk            <- 2L
fs_use_lasso       <- TRUE
fs_use_grf         <- TRUE
fs_is_RCT          <- TRUE
fs_vi_grf_min      <- -0.2
fs_dmin_grf        <- 0
fs_cont_cutoff     <- 4L

# ─── Pareto-frontier diagnostic parameters ──────────────────────────────
# Drives compute_frontier_cis(), plot_pareto_frontier(),
# pareto_frontier_table(), and explain_pareto_selection() in the
# post-hoc selection diagnostic section.
# NB: with sg_focus = "effMaxSG" and selection_rule = "both", the rule
# selects from the intersection of the effect-size neighborhood (within
# `effect_neighborhood` of the maximum) and the Pareto-non-dominated set
# on (effect, N).  The selected subgroup is typically a frontier member.
# The frontier is shown here both as the selection criterion AND as a
# diagnostic of the candidate trade-off space.
# For OR (ratio-scale), the effect axis is auto-rendered on log scale
# by plot_pareto_frontier(); leave xlim = NULL for auto bounds.
frontier_params <- list(
  n_splits      = 1000L,
  seed          = 1L,
  xlim          = c(0.35,10),       # auto (OR auto-detected as ratio scale)
  digits        = 2L
)

# ─── GRF standalone parameters (beneficial scale) ──────────────────────
grf_outcome_type   <- "binary"
grf_effect_measure <- "OR"
grf_dmin_grf       <- 0.1    # on the RD scale for binary outcomes
                             # (e.g., 0.10 = 10 percentage-point absolute
                             # difference in event rates)
grf_maxdepth       <- 2L
grf_RCT            <- TRUE
grf_sg_criterion   <- "mDiff"
grf_tune           <- FALSE

# ─── Bootstrap (gated; demo by default) ────────────────────────────────
run_bootstrap <- TRUE
NB <- 20L     # PRESSURE-TEST DEMO. Set to 500-2000 for production.

# ─── Cross-Validation (gated; demo by default) ─────────────────────────
run_cv <- TRUE
Kfolds_cv <- 10L  # PRESSURE-TEST DEMO. 10-fold CV. For LOO, set to nrow(fs_result$df.est).
                  # Production: 10-fold is standard; consider forestsearch_tenfold()
                  # with sims = 50-100 for repeated K-fold stability assessment.

# ─── Leave-One-Out CV (gated; demo by default) ─────────────────────────
# LOO runs forestsearch() once per observation (N folds).  Comparable in
# cost to K-fold * N/K, but well-tolerated on samples up to ~1000.
# Set FALSE to skip; toggles independently of run_cv.
run_loo <- FALSE

# ─── Numeric Precision ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Two-stage precision control (Reading-C design):
# - construction_digits: upstream sprintf precision in the bootstrap and
#   CV table builders. Acts as a CEILING for downstream display: values
#   rounded here cannot be recovered later. Default 4 provides headroom.
# - display_digits: precision rendered in user-facing tables.
#   summarize_bootstrap_results() parses construction-time strings and
#   reformats at this precision, which must be <= construction_digits.
#   sg_tables() applies it via ndecimals; cv_summary_tables() applies
#   it via digits.
construction_digits <- 2L
display_digits      <- 2L

# ─── Combined Forest Plot ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Capstone visualization that integrates fs_result, fs_bc (if bootstrap),
# and fs_kfold_result (if CV).  Always rendered; CV/bootstrap annotations
# appear conditionally on the run_* flags.
run_forestplot <- TRUE
```


# Data Preparation

## Treatment Assignment

```{r data-treat}
# ACTG175: arm 1 = ZDV+ddI (experimental), arm 3 = ddI (control)
actg_df <- subset(speff2trial::ACTG175, arms %in% c(1L, 3L))
actg_df$id <- seq_len(nrow(actg_df))

# Treatment: ZDV+ddI = 1, ddI = 0 (NO switching)
actg_df$treat <- ifelse(actg_df$arms == 1L, 1L, 0L)
```

## Outcome Construction

```{r data-outcomes}
# Drop subjects missing the week-20 CD4 measurement
actg_df <- actg_df[!is.na(actg_df$cd420), ]

# Beneficial scale: CD4 improvement indicator (1 = improved, higher = better)
actg_df$y_binary_pos <- as.integer(actg_df$cd420 > actg_df$cd40)

# Adverse scale: NO improvement indicator (1 = did not improve, higher = worse)
actg_df$y_binary_neg <- 1L - actg_df$y_binary_pos

outcome_vars <- c("y_binary_neg", "y_binary_pos")
```

## Covariates

```{r data-covariates}
# Coerce binary indicators to factors (analyst does not know true cuts
# for continuous covariates; ForestSearch handles those internally)
for (v in bin_vars) actg_df[[v]] <- as.factor(actg_df[[v]])

cat("Continuous candidates:", paste(cont_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Binary candidates:    ", paste(bin_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

## Baseline Characteristics

```{r baseline-table}
create_summary_table(
  data = actg_df,
  treat_var = treat.name,
  table_title = "ACTG175 Baseline Characteristics and Outcomes by Treatment Arm",
  vars_continuous = c(outcome_vars,cont_vars),
  vars_categorical = bin_vars,
  font_size = 12
)
```

## ITT Analysis

```{r itt-analysis}
# Adverse-scale ITT OR (y_binary_neg = no improvement; OR > 1 = treatment
# increases the odds of no improvement = harm)
itt_neg <- glm(y_binary_neg ~ treat, data = actg_df, family = binomial)

# Beneficial-scale ITT OR (y_binary_pos = improvement; OR > 1 = treatment
# increases the odds of improvement = benefit)
itt_pos <- glm(y_binary_pos ~ treat, data = actg_df, family = binomial)

# Helper to print OR / log-OR / 95% CI / p-value
print_or <- function(fit, label) {
  beta  <- coef(fit)["treat"]
  se    <- summary(fit)$coefficients["treat", "Std. Error"]
  z     <- beta / se
  p     <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
  or    <- exp(beta)
  ci_lo <- exp(beta - qnorm(0.975) * se)
  ci_hi <- exp(beta + qnorm(0.975) * se)
  cat(sprintf("=== ITT Odds Ratio, %s ===\n", label))
  cat(sprintf("  log-OR (treat): %7.4f  (SE %.4f)\n", beta, se))
  cat(sprintf("  OR:             %6.3f  (95%% CI: %.3f, %.3f)\n",
              or, ci_lo, ci_hi))
  cat(sprintf("  p-value:        %.4f\n", p))
}

print_or(itt_neg, "adverse scale (y_binary_neg)")
cat("\n")
print_or(itt_pos, "beneficial scale (y_binary_pos)")

cat("\nNote: y_binary_neg = 1 - y_binary_pos, so the two log-ORs are\n")
cat("equal in magnitude with opposite signs (likewise the two ORs are\n")
cat("reciprocals of each other).\n")
```


# Part I: ForestSearch (Adverse Scale) {#sec-fs}

## Rationale

ForestSearch operates on the adverse scale (`y_binary_neg`, indicator of
NO improvement) with `adverse_outcome = TRUE`. An OR above
`fs_or_threshold` indicates the treatment **increases the odds of
no improvement** in that subgroup (harm). No outcome flip is applied;
the screening threshold is on the OR scale directly.

## ForestSearch Parameters

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
**API note: GLM-natural vocabulary.**  This template uses the
GLM-natural parameter names introduced in forestsearch 0.2.0:

- `sg_focus = "effMaxSG"` (alias for the legacy `"hrMaxSG"`)
- `effect.threshold` (alias for `hr.threshold`)
- `consistency.threshold` (alias for `hr.consistency`)

The `"eff*"` and `effect.*` forms read more naturally for GLM
outcomes (continuous MD, binary OR/RR/RD, count IRR) where there is
no hazard ratio.  The legacy `"hr*"` and `hr.*` forms continue to
work and produce identical results.  See `NEWS.md` for the full
list of aliases.
:::

| Parameter | Value | Description |
|-----------|-------|-------------|
| `effect_measure` | `OR` | Odds ratio (binary) |
| `effect.threshold` | 1.25 | Screening OR threshold (adverse scale) |
| `consistency.threshold` | 1.0 | Per-split consistency OR threshold |
| `pconsistency.threshold` | 0.80 | Required consistency rate across splits |
| `maxk` | 2 | Maximum factors per subgroup |
| `n.min` | 60 | Minimum subgroup size |
| `d0.min`, `d1.min` | 10 | Minimum sample size per arm |
| `fs.splits` | 500 | Random 50/50 splits for consistency |
| `sg_focus` | `effMaxSG` | Effect-neighborhood focus (max-N tiebreaker) |
| `selection_rule` | `both` | Intersection of neighborhood and Pareto sets |

## Running ForestSearch

```{r forestsearch-fs}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

t0 <- proc.time()

fs_result <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis      = actg_df,
  confounders.name = confounders.name,
  outcome.name     = adverse_outcome,
  event.name       = adverse_outcome,    # binary: outcome IS the event
  treat.name       = treat.name,
  id.name          = id.name,
  # GLM parameters
  outcome_type     = fs_outcome_type,
  effect_measure   = fs_effect_measure,
  adverse_outcome  = TRUE,
  seedit           = analysis_seed,
  # Threshold parameters (OR scale)
  effect.threshold       = fs_or_threshold,
  consistency.threshold  = fs_or_consistency,
  pconsistency.threshold = fs_pconsistency,
  # Search configuration
  sg_focus         = fs_sg_focus,
  selection_rule   = fs_selection_rule,
  max_subgroups_search = fs_max_subgroups,
  use_twostage     = TRUE,    
  conf.cont_jcuts           = list(cd40 = 10, wtkg = 10),
  # Factor selection
  use_grf          = fs_use_grf,
  return_selected_cuts_only = TRUE,
  use_lasso        = fs_use_lasso,
  cut_type         = "default",
  # Subgroup constraints
  maxk             = fs_maxk,
  n.min            = fs_n_min,
  d0.min           = fs_d0_min,
  d1.min           = fs_d1_min,
  # Consistency evaluation
  fs.splits        = fs_splits,
  # Parallel processing
  parallel_args    = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  ),
  # Output options
  show_candidate_summary = TRUE,
  details          = TRUE,
  plot.sg          = FALSE,    # KM not applicable; use plot_sg_glm_outcomes()
  is.RCT           = fs_is_RCT,
  vi.grf.min       = fs_vi_grf_min,
  dmin.grf         = fs_dmin_grf,
  cont.cutoff      = fs_cont_cutoff,
  tune_grf         = grf_tune,
  quiet            = FALSE
)

plan("sequential"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
timings$fs <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]

cat("\nForestSearch (adverse scale) completed in",
    round(timings$fs, 1), "seconds\n")
```

## Selection Diagnostic: Pareto Frontier

Post-hoc diagnostic showing all passing candidates on the (OR, N) plane.

::: {.callout-note}
**Context for `sg_focus = "effMaxSG"` with `selection_rule = "both"`.**
The rule selects from the intersection of two sets: candidates within
`effect_neighborhood` of the maximum effect (the "in-band" set), AND
candidates on the Pareto frontier in (effect, N).  Among that
intersection, the rule picks the largest-N candidate.

The selected subgroup is therefore typically a frontier member,
and the frontier plot serves both as the selection geometry AND as a
diagnostic showing the alternatives the rule considered (and ruled
out).  Compare this to the comparison vignette, which shows what
happens when `selection_rule` is varied with all else fixed.

For OR outcomes the effect axis is auto-rendered on log scale by
`plot_pareto_frontier()` and `pareto_frontier_table()` (auto-detected
from `fs_result$effect_measure`); the rendered values are on the
natural OR scale.
:::

```{r fs-pareto}
# Formatted gt table; selected subgroup is highlighted and marked with ★.
# Works uniformly for survival (HR) and GLM (OR, RR, IRR, RD, IRD, MD)
# outcomes — effect-column label and scale derived from
# fs_result$effect_measure.  For OR, the effect column is exponentiated
# for display and the band test is on the natural OR scale.

# 1. Compute the CIs once (this is the expensive step, ~1-3 min).
#    Parameters come from frontier_params in the Analysis Configuration.
ci_tab <- compute_frontier_cis(
  fs_result,
  n_splits = frontier_params$n_splits,
  seed     = frontier_params$seed
)

# 2. Plot, with split-derived CI bars overlaid; same intervals as the table.
p_pareto <- plot_pareto_frontier(
  fs_result,
  ci_table  = ci_tab,
  show_band = TRUE,
  xlim      = frontier_params$xlim
)
print(p_pareto)

# 3. Render the table. Pass the same ci_tab so the table and plot show
#    identical intervals.
pareto_frontier_table(
  fs_result,
  ci_table = ci_tab,
  digits   = frontier_params$digits
)
```


### Selection Narrative

`explain_pareto_selection()` describes the chosen subgroup relative to
the non-dominated alternatives on the frontier.  Under `effMaxSG` with
`selection_rule = "both"`, the winner is a frontier member that also
sits in the effect-size band; the "losers" are frontier candidates
that fall outside the band (high-N candidates with weaker effect).
The narrative names both the criterion and the runner-up.

```{r fs-pareto-explain, results = "asis"}
cat(explain_pareto_selection(fs_result, ci_table = ci_tab))
```


```{r fs-pareto-data, eval = FALSE}
# Programmatic access — two paths.

# (a) Frontier table with pre-formatted CI strings, one row per frontier
#     member.  CI columns ("Naive 95% CI", "Split ~ 95% CI",
#     "FSBC ~ 95% CI") are character strings like "(1.45, 2.87)".
pareto_frontier_table(
  fs_result,
  ci_table = ci_tab,
  format   = "data.table",
  digits   = frontier_params$digits
)

# (b) Rich post-consistency view: ALL passing candidates (not just the
#     frontier), with on_frontier and (where applicable) in_band flag
#     columns added.  Provides programmatic access to the same content
#     as the in-flight summary printed by forestsearch().
pareto_frontier_table(
  fs_result,
  ci_table          = ci_tab,
  include_dominated = TRUE,
  format            = "data.table",
  digits            = frontier_params$digits
)

# (c) Raw numeric CIs: keyed data.table with one row per frontier
#     member.  Same content as (a) but each bound is a numeric column
#     (naive_lcl, naive_ucl, split_lcl, split_ucl, fsbc_estimate,
#     fsbc_lcl, fsbc_ucl, plus split_sd and n_valid_splits).  This is
#     what step 1 of fs-pareto produced.
ci_tab
```


## Bootstrap Bias Correction

Bootstrap bias correction adjusts the FS point estimate for the optimism
inherent in data-driven subgroup identification. The bootstrap pipeline
auto-detects the `OR` effect column from `fs_result` and produces
bias-corrected OR estimates with bootstrap distributions and diagnostics.

::: {.callout-note}
**Demo mode**: `NB = 20` for pressure-testing the pipeline end-to-end.
Production runs should use `NB = 500–2000`. Set `run_bootstrap = FALSE`
in the parameters chunk to skip this section entirely.
:::

```{r fs-bootstrap-run}
#| eval: !expr run_bootstrap

t0 <- proc.time()

fs_bc <- forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture(
  fs.est = fs_result,
  nb_boots = NB,
  show_three = FALSE,
  details = FALSE,
  digits = construction_digits,
  parallel_args = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  )
)

plan("sequential"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
timings$bootstrap <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]

cat("\nBootstrap completed in", round(timings$bootstrap / 60, 2), "minutes",
    sprintf("(NB = %d, n_cores = %d)\n", NB, n_cores))
```

### Bootstrap Summary

```{r fs-bootstrap-summary}
#| eval: !expr run_bootstrap

# Note: est.scale only affects the legacy HR-flavored caption helper; the
# OR column (with bias-corrected OR*) is auto-detected from FSsg_tab.
fs_summaries <- summarize_bootstrap_results(
  sgharm       = fs_result$sg.harm,
  boot_results = fs_bc,
  create_plots = TRUE,
  est.scale    = "hr",
  digits       = display_digits
)

fs_summaries$table
```

### Bootstrap Diagnostics

```{r fs-bootstrap-diagnostics}

fs_summaries$diagnostics_table_gt
```

### Subgroup Agreement

```{r fs-bootstrap-agreement}
  fs_summaries$subgroup_summary$original_agreement
}
```

```{r fs-bootstrap-factors}

  fs_summaries$subgroup_summary$factor_presence
}
```

```{r fs-bootstrap-plots}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distributions of OR for H (questionable) and Hc (recommend)"

  fs_summaries$plots$H_distribution + fs_summaries$plots$Hc_distribution
}
```

## Cross-Validation

K-fold cross-validation assesses the **stability** of the FS pipeline by
re-running ForestSearch on each leave-out fold and comparing the
identified subgroup to the full-data analysis. Per-fold results are
aggregated into agreement metrics (sensitivity for H and Hc) and
finding rates.

::: {.callout-note}
**Demo mode**: `Kfolds_cv = 10` for pressure-testing the CV pipeline
end-to-end. Production runs typically use 10-fold CV; for repeated
K-fold stability assessment, see `forestsearch_tenfold(sims = 50, Kfolds = 10)`.
Set `run_cv = FALSE` in the parameters chunk to skip this section.
:::

```{r fs-cv-run}
#| eval: !expr run_cv

t0 <- proc.time()

fs_kfold_result <- forestsearch_Kfold(
  fs.est        = fs_result,
  Kfolds        = Kfolds_cv,
  seedit        = analysis_seed,
  parallel_args = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  ),
  details       = FALSE
)

plan("sequential"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
timings$cv <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]

cat("\nCross-validation completed in", round(timings$cv / 60, 2), "minutes",
    sprintf("(Kfolds = %d, n_cores = %d)\n", Kfolds_cv, n_cores))
```

### CV Summary

```{r fs-cv-summary-text}
#| eval: !expr run_cv

# One-line summary: finding rate + agreement
cat(cv_summary_text(fs_kfold_result, est.scale = "hr"), "\n")
cat(sprintf("Subgroup found in %.0f%% of %d folds.\n",
            100 * fs_kfold_result$prop_SG_found, Kfolds_cv))
```

### CV Tables

```{r fs-cv-tables}

kfold_out <- forestsearch_KfoldOut(fs_kfold_result, outall = TRUE,
                                   digits = construction_digits)
cv_tabs   <- cv_summary_tables(
  kfold_out,
  title    = "ACTG175 Cross-Validation Summary (Binary, OR)",
  subtitle = sprintf("ITT and Subgroup Estimates: Full Analysis (FA) vs %d-fold (Kf)",
                     Kfolds_cv),
  digits   = display_digits,
  use_gt   = TRUE
)

cv_tabs$combined_table
```

```{r fs-cv-metrics}
  cv_tabs$metrics_table
}
```


## Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation

Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation is the limiting case of K-fold CV
where each observation is held out once. It is the most thorough form
of CV, eliminating fold-assignment randomness, and is the appropriate
benchmark when sample size is small enough to make `N` re-fits
tractable.

::: {.callout-note}
**Cost**: LOO runs `forestsearch()` once per observation. Toggleable
independently from K-fold via `run_loo` in the parameters chunk. On
samples up to roughly 1000 the cost is well-tolerated with parallel
workers; beyond that, K-fold is preferred.
:::

```{r fs-loo-run}
#| eval: !expr run_loo

t0 <- proc.time()

# LOO is triggered by Kfolds = N (the function default behavior at
# forestsearch_cross_validation.R:109).  We pass it explicitly here for
# clarity.
N_loo <- nrow(fs_result$df.est)

fs_loo_result <- forestsearch_Kfold(
  fs.est        = fs_result,
  Kfolds        = N_loo,
  seedit        = analysis_seed,
  parallel_args = list(
    plan = "multisession",
    workers = n_cores,
    show_message = TRUE
  ),
  details       = FALSE
)

plan("sequential"); gc(verbose = FALSE)
timings$loo <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]

cat("\nLOO completed in", round(timings$loo / 60, 2), "minutes",
    sprintf("(N folds = %d, n_cores = %d)\n", N_loo, n_cores))
```

### LOO Summary

```{r fs-loo-summary-text}
#| eval: !expr run_loo

cat(cv_summary_text(fs_loo_result, est.scale = "hr"), "\n")
cat(sprintf("Subgroup found in %.0f%% of %d folds.\n",
            100 * fs_loo_result$prop_SG_found, N_loo))
```

### LOO Tables

The `cv_summary_tables()` helper returns five publication-ready `gt`
tables. The first is the combined ITT + subgroup view; the next three
are component estimation tables (ITT, full-analysis subgroup, LOO
subgroup) that show the underlying treatment-effect estimates with
confidence intervals.

```{r fs-loo-tables}
#| eval: !expr run_loo

loo_out  <- forestsearch_KfoldOut(fs_loo_result, outall = TRUE,
                                  digits = construction_digits)
loo_tabs <- cv_summary_tables(
  loo_out,
  title    = "ACTG175 Leave-One-Out CV Summary (Binary, OR)",
  subtitle = sprintf("ITT and Subgroup Estimates: Full Analysis (FA) vs LOO (N=%d)",
                     N_loo),
  digits   = display_digits,
  use_gt   = TRUE
)
```

## Combined Forest Plot

Capstone visualization integrating the FS-identified subgroup with
bootstrap-bias-corrected MD (when bootstrap was run) and cross-
validation agreement annotations (when CV was run).

```{r fs-forestplot}
#| eval: !expr run_forestplot
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Forest plot of ITT and identified subgroup; OR on the adverse scale (no improvement)"

# Build fs_results list dynamically based on what's been computed.
fs_results_list <- list(fs.est = fs_result)

if (exists("fs_bc")) {
  fs_results_list$fs_bc <- fs_bc
}
# Forest plot accepts one CV source in the fs_kfold slot.  Prefer
# K-fold; fall back to LOO if K-fold wasn't run but LOO was.
cv_label_for_plot <- NULL
if (exists("fs_kfold_result")) {
  fs_results_list$fs_kfold <- fs_kfold_result
  cv_label_for_plot <- sprintf("%d-fold CV", Kfolds_cv)
} else if (exists("fs_loo_result")) {
  fs_results_list$fs_kfold <- fs_loo_result
  cv_label_for_plot <- "LOO CV"
}

# For binary outcomes, event.name = outcome.name (the binary indicator is
# its own event).  xlog = TRUE for OR (ratio scale, log axis).
forest_obj <- plot_subgroup_results_forestplot(
  fs_results     = fs_results_list,
  df_analysis    = actg_df,
  outcome.name   = adverse_outcome,
  event.name     = adverse_outcome,
  treat.name     = treat.name,
  E.name         = "ZDV+ddI",
  C.name         = "ddI",
  outcome_type   = fs_outcome_type,
  effect_measure = fs_effect_measure,
  xlog           = TRUE,                 # OR is ratio scale -> log axis
  arrow_text     = c("Favors ZDV+ddI", "Favors ddI"),
  title_text     = "ACTG175 Subgroup Results — Binary (OR, adverse scale)",
  show_cv_metrics = !is.null(cv_label_for_plot),
  cv_source      = "kfold",
  xlim_method    = "data"
)

render_forestplot(forest_obj)

if (!is.null(cv_label_for_plot)) {
  cat(sprintf("\nCV annotations source: %s.\n", cv_label_for_plot))
}
```


# Part II: GRF Standalone (Beneficial Scale) {#sec-grf}

## Rationale

GRF operates on the beneficial scale (`y_binary_pos`, indicator of CD4
improvement) with `adverse_outcome = FALSE` (the default). A negative
CATE means the treatment **decreases the probability of improvement** in
that subgroup — harm via insufficient benefit. This is the natural
complement to the FS analysis on the adverse scale: same outcome data,
opposite encoding, and a different model class (causal forest with
policy-tree subgroup extraction).

For binary outcomes the per-subject CATE from `grf::causal_forest()` is
on the **risk-difference (RD) scale**: \\(\\widehat{\\tau}_i =
\\hat{P}(Y_i=1 \\mid T=1, X_i) - \\hat{P}(Y_i=1 \\mid T=0, X_i)\\),
bounded in \\([-1, 1]\\).  The `dmin.grf` threshold is interpreted on
this same RD scale (e.g., `dmin.grf = 0.10` requires at least a 10
percentage-point absolute difference in event rates).  The effect-measure
label `"OR"` controls how the FS-side estimation and reporting step
renders the subgroup contrast; the GRF CATE itself remains on the RD
scale internally.

## Running GRF

```{r grf-run}
t0 <- proc.time()

grf_result <- grf.subg.harm.glm(
  data             = actg_df,
  confounders.name = confounders.name,
  outcome.name     = beneficial_outcome,
  treat.name       = treat.name,
  id.name          = id.name,
  outcome_type     = grf_outcome_type,
  effect_measure   = grf_effect_measure,
  dmin.grf         = grf_dmin_grf,
  maxdepth         = grf_maxdepth,
  RCT              = grf_RCT,
  sg.criterion     = grf_sg_criterion,
  details          = TRUE
)

timings$grf <- (proc.time() - t0)["elapsed"]
cat("\nGRF (beneficial scale) completed in",
    round(timings$grf, 1), "seconds\n")
```

## Policy Trees

```{r grf-trees}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Policy trees from GRF (depth 1 and 2)"

if (!is.null(grf_result$trees)) {
  oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
  if (length(grf_result$trees) >= 1 && !is.null(grf_result$trees[[1]])) {
    plot(grf_result$trees[[1]],
         leaf.labels = c("Control", "Treat"), main = "Depth 1")
  }
  if (length(grf_result$trees) >= 2 && !is.null(grf_result$trees[[2]])) {
    plot(grf_result$trees[[2]],
         leaf.labels = c("Control", "Treat"), main = "Depth 2")
  }
  par(oldpar)
} else {
  cat("GRF: no policy trees available.\n")
}
```

## Identified Subgroup Definition

```{r grf-subgroup}
if (!is.null(grf_result$sg.harm.id) && length(grf_result$sg.harm.id) > 0) {
  grf_H <- grf_result$data$treat.recommend == 0
  cat("Identified subgroup (H, GRF beneficial):",
      paste(grf_result$sg.harm.id, collapse = " & "), "\n")
  cat(sprintf("Subgroup size: %d (%.1f%% of ITT)\n",
              sum(grf_H), 100 * mean(grf_H)))
  cat(sprintf("CATE(H):  %+6.3f  (RD: P(improve|T=1) - P(improve|T=0) in H)\n",
              grf_result$cate_sg))
  cat(sprintf("CATE(Hc): %+6.3f\n", grf_result$cate_sgc))
} else {
  cat("GRF: no subgroup identified.\n")
}
```

## GRF Variable Importance

GRF reports per-covariate variable importance from the causal forest,
quantifying each covariate's contribution to splitting decisions in the
treatment-effect estimation. Higher values indicate stronger influence
on detected heterogeneity. Note this differs from prediction-importance
in standard random forests; here it reflects relevance to **CATE
estimation**, not to the marginal outcome.

```{r grf-varimp}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "GRF variable importance from the causal forest"

if (!is.null(grf_result$grf_varimp) && length(grf_result$grf_varimp) > 0) {
  vi <- grf_result$grf_varimp
  vi_df <- data.frame(
    variable   = names(vi),
    importance = unname(vi)
  )
  # Order ascending so largest appears at top after coord_flip()
  vi_df <- vi_df[order(vi_df$importance), ]
  vi_df$variable <- factor(vi_df$variable, levels = vi_df$variable)

  ggplot(vi_df, aes(x = variable, y = importance)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      x        = NULL,
      y        = "GRF variable importance",
      title    = "GRF Variable Importance",
      subtitle = "Higher = more influence on treatment-effect heterogeneity"
    )
} else {
  cat("GRF variable importance not available.\n")
}
```

## CATE Distribution

Per-subject conditional average treatment effects (CATE) are estimated
from GRF's double-robust scores: \\( \\widehat{\\tau}_i = \\Gamma_{1,i} - \\Gamma_{0,i} \\),
where \\( \\Gamma_0 \\) and \\( \\Gamma_1 \\) are the doubly robust outcome
predictions under control and treatment. For binary outcomes the CATE
is on the **risk-difference (RD) scale**: positive CATE means the
treatment increases the probability of improvement (benefit); negative
CATE means it decreases the probability (harm via insufficient
improvement). The histogram below shows the empirical CATE distribution
across subjects, colored by GRF-assigned subgroup membership. Bounded in
\\([-1, 1]\\) in principle, though typical CATE magnitudes are smaller
(±0.1 to ±0.3 absolute probability difference).

```{r grf-cate-distribution}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Per-subject CATE distribution from GRF, colored by H / Hc membership"

if (!is.null(grf_result$dr_scores) &&
    !is.null(grf_result$data$treat.recommend)) {

  cate_per_subject <- grf_result$dr_scores[, 2L] -
                      grf_result$dr_scores[, 1L]
  group_label <- ifelse(grf_result$data$treat.recommend == 0,
                        "H (questionable)",
                        "H\u1d9c (recommend)")
  cate_df <- data.frame(
    cate  = cate_per_subject,
    group = factor(group_label,
                   levels = c("H (questionable)", "H\u1d9c (recommend)"))
  )

  ggplot(cate_df, aes(x = cate, fill = group)) +
    geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", bins = 30,
                   color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey30") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = grf_result$cate_sg,
               linetype = "dotted", color = "coral", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = grf_result$cate_sgc,
               linetype = "dotted", color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(
      "H (questionable)"     = "coral",
      "H\u1d9c (recommend)"  = "steelblue"
    )) +
    labs(
      x        = "Per-subject CATE: P(Y=1|T=1) - P(Y=1|T=0)  (RD scale)",
      y        = "Count",
      title    = "GRF CATE Distribution",
      subtitle = paste0("Dotted lines: subgroup-mean CATE(H) = ",
                        sprintf("%+.3f", grf_result$cate_sg),
                        ", CATE(H\u1d9c) = ",
                        sprintf("%+.3f", grf_result$cate_sgc),
                        ".  Negative CATE = harm via insufficient improvement."),
      fill     = "Subgroup"
    )
} else {
  cat("GRF DR-scores or treat.recommend not available.\n")
}
```

## Treatment Effect Estimates

```{r grf-estimates}
grf_tabs <- sg_tables(grf_result, ndecimals = display_digits, which_df = "est")
grf_tabs$tab_estimates
```

## Subgroup Outcome Visualization

```{r grf-glm-plot}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Rate of CD4 improvement by treatment arm and identified subgroup (GRF, beneficial scale)"

# plot_sg_glm_outcomes() expects an fs.est-shaped object with df.est and
# sg.harm.  GRF returns `data` and `sg.harm.id`, so we wrap them in a
# minimal shim list.  All other arguments are passed explicitly so no
# auto-detection from the shim is required.
grf_shim <- list(
  df.est         = grf_result$data,
  outcome_type   = grf_result$outcome_type,
  effect_measure = grf_result$effect_measure,
  sg.harm        = grf_result$sg.harm.id
)

grf_plot <- plot_sg_glm_outcomes(
  fs.est         = grf_shim,
  outcome.name   = beneficial_outcome,
  treat.name     = treat.name,
  effect_measure = grf_effect_measure,
  outcome_type   = grf_outcome_type,
  E.name         = "ZDV+ddI",
  C.name         = "ddI",
  show_itt       = TRUE,
  show_effect    = TRUE,
  verbose        = TRUE
)
```


# Part III: Cross-Method Comparison {#sec-compare}

The two analyses define H differently:

- FS uses the adverse scale (`y_binary_neg`, `OR > c1` = harm).
- GRF uses the beneficial scale (`y_binary_pos`, CATE below 0 = harm).

Both classify subjects as H (`treat.recommend == 0`) when they meet their
respective harm criterion, so per-subject membership is directly
comparable. The cross-tabulation below reports raw agreement and Cohen's
κ.

```{r cross-method}
sg_comparison <- compare_fs_subgroups(
  fs1     = fs_result,
  fs2     = grf_result,
  label1  = "FS (adverse)",
  label2  = "GRF (beneficial)",
  id.name = id.name,
  subgroup_notation = "harm",
  title   = "FS-Adverse vs GRF-Beneficial: Subgroup Membership"
)

sg_comparison$table
```

```{r cross-method-print}
cat("=== Concordance summary ===\n")
cat(sprintf("Agreement:    %.1f%%\n",
            100 * sg_comparison$concordance$agreement))
if (!is.null(sg_comparison$concordance$kappa)) {
  cat(sprintf("Cohen's kappa: %.3f\n",
              sg_comparison$concordance$kappa))
}
```


# Computational Timing

```{r timing-summary}
timings$total <- (proc.time() - t_vignette_start)["elapsed"]

components <- c("ForestSearch (adverse)", "GRF (beneficial)")
seconds    <- c(timings$fs,             timings$grf)

if (run_bootstrap && !is.null(timings$bootstrap)) {
  components <- c(components, "Bootstrap (FS)")
  seconds    <- c(seconds,    timings$bootstrap)
}

if (run_cv && !is.null(timings$cv)) {
  components <- c(components, "Cross-Validation (FS)")
  seconds    <- c(seconds,    timings$cv)
}

if (run_loo && !is.null(timings$loo)) {
  components <- c(components, "Leave-One-Out CV (FS)")
  seconds    <- c(seconds,    timings$loo)
}

components <- c(components, "Total")
seconds    <- c(seconds,    timings$total)

timing_df <- data.frame(
  Analysis = components,
  Seconds  = unname(seconds),
  Minutes  = unname(seconds) / 60
)

gt(timing_df) |>
  tab_header(title = "Computational Timing") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Seconds, Minutes), decimals = 2) |>
  cols_label(
    Analysis = "Component",
    Seconds  = "Time (sec)",
    Minutes  = "Time (min)"
  )
```
